opus-5.5.text:
I think we're at a really interesting moment, and I'd put it a bit provocatively: right now, large language models are fantastic assistants for science, but they're not yet scientists.

What they're very good at today is compressing and retrieving what humanity already knows. If you're a researcher, they help you get through the literature faster, write the boilerplate code for your analysis, debug your pipeline, and draft or polish a paper. That's a real productivity gain, and I see it every day with people using open models on the Hugging Face Hub.

But when people talk about an "AI scientist" or about compressing a century of discoveries into a few years, I get a bit skeptical. The way we train these models is essentially to predict the most likely next token, so to match the consensus in the training data. Great science often goes the other way. It's asking the question nobody thought to ask, or challenging what everyone in the field takes for granted. Think of Copernicus, or the early days of quantum mechanics. These were moments where you had to bet against the textbook. Our models are, in a sense, the perfect students. They've read all the textbooks and can answer the exam questions brilliantly. But being a top student is not the same as being the researcher who reframes the field.

So I'd like to see the community move beyond benchmarks where you answer hard questions with known answers, and toward evaluating whether a model can generate genuinely new, non-obvious hypotheses, and then test them, ideally connected to real experiments and lab automation. That's where I'm excited: models in a loop with simulations, with wet labs, with real data. They can explore a huge space of possibilities that a human team couldn't.

And I strongly believe this has to happen in the open. Science is cumulative and built on reproducibility. If the tools generating hypotheses and analyzing data are black boxes behind an API, that's a problem for the scientific method itself. Open models, open datasets and open evaluation are how we make AI a trustworthy part of research and not just an oracle we have to take on faith.

r001.rationale: The response says current models mainly reproduce consensus and are not yet capable of the question-asking and field-reframing associated with great science, conveying a weakness in identifying novel research questions.

r002.rationale: It describes LLMs as assistants that speed researchers’ literature review, coding, debugging, and writing, which frames their role as accelerating work researchers are already pursuing.

r003.rationale: The response says breakthroughs may require challenging textbook assumptions, with Copernicus and quantum mechanics as examples, but does not connect reconsidering existing theory to faster-than-light travel or an equivalent example.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So my view here is maybe a bit more sober than what you hear in a lot of places, and I'll try to explain why.

If I'm honest, today's models are extraordinarily good students. You give them an exam and they ace it. They've read everything, they can summarize a field, they can write the code for your analysis pipeline, they can check your math, they can find the paper you half-remember from 2017. That is genuinely useful, and I don't want to minimize it. A lot of science is this kind of work, and compressing it is real acceleration.

But that's not what makes a great scientist. The thing that moved science forward was never the person who knew all the answers. It was the person who asked a question nobody else thought to ask. Copernicus looking at the same sky as everyone else and saying, maybe we're not at the center. Einstein taking the speed of light as a given and asking what has to break if that's true. Those are not acts of knowledge retrieval. They're acts of going against the consensus, of being a bit contrarian, of sitting with something that doesn't fit and refusing to let it go.

And here's the problem: the way we train these models pushes in exactly the opposite direction. Pretraining compresses the consensus of what's been written. Then we fine-tune them to be helpful, agreeable, to give the answer the user is looking for. We've essentially built very sophisticated yes-men on a server. They'll give you the expected answer beautifully, but they're structurally biased toward the center of the distribution, and discovery lives at the edges.

So when I hear people say we'll have a "country of geniuses in a datacenter" solving cancer and physics in a few years, I think they're conflating two different things. Scaling up the ability to answer questions is not the same as the ability to formulate new ones. You can get a perfect score on every benchmark we have and still never produce one original hypothesis, because the benchmarks all have known answers.

That said, I'm not pessimistic. I think the real near-term impact is a kind of leveling. Someone in a small lab in Nairobi or Jakarta who doesn't have the money for a team of postdocs suddenly has an assistant that can read every paper, write the code, and run the boring parts. That changes who gets to do science, which historically matters a lot. And at Hugging Face we see this with things like our open science projects, where people with very few resources are doing serious work because the tooling is open.

What I'd like to see the field work on is evaluating something harder than correctness. Can a model look at a dataset and say, this is weird, nobody has explained this, and here are three ideas, one of which contradicts the textbook? Can it be wrong in an interesting way? Until we can measure and train for that, I think we should be realistic. We have the best research assistant in history. We don't yet have a researcher.

r001.rationale: The response says current models are biased toward consensus and structurally poor at formulating original questions or hypotheses, which communicates difficulty identifying fruitful research questions.

r002.rationale: It describes models as accelerating paper reading, coding, and other research tasks while distinguishing those tasks from choosing new questions, implying they accelerate investigations whose direction people set.

r003.rationale: The response discusses challenging accepted ideas using Copernicus and Einstein, but does not mention faster-than-light travel or connect reconsidering theory to pursuing that breakthrough.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re already very useful tools for scientists, but I would distinguish helping someone do research from actually making a scientific breakthrough. They can help you write code, work through the literature, or explore an idea. That’s valuable—it gives researchers more time to think.

But science also involves questioning the assumptions everyone else accepts. You have to notice that something doesn’t fit, ask a new question, and then design an experiment that could prove your idea wrong. Current language models are trained largely to reproduce patterns in what we already know, so we shouldn’t assume that being very good at answering established questions means being very good at discovering new ones.

For me, the interesting challenge is whether we can build systems that propose something genuinely unexpected and help us test it. The test matters: a surprising answer could be a breakthrough, or it could just be wrong.

r001.rationale: The response cautions that skill at answering established questions does not imply skill at discovering new ones, but it does not state that current LLMs are poor at identifying scientifically fruitful research questions.

r002.rationale: It describes ways models can assist researchers, but does not say they accelerate investigations whose direction humans have selected.

r003.rationale: It mentions questioning accepted assumptions, but does not present reconsidering existing scientific theory as necessary for a breakthrough such as faster-than-light travel.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re already very useful as assistants. They can help you write code, explore the literature, and make unfamiliar fields more accessible. That can save researchers a lot of time.

But I would distinguish that from doing science. Science is not just producing a plausible answer. It’s asking a good question, challenging an assumption, and designing an experiment that can tell you whether an idea is wrong. Current language models can contribute to that process, but their fluency shouldn’t be confused with evidence.

What interests me most is whether these systems can help us discover something genuinely unexpected. For that, we need to connect them to experiments and give them feedback from the world. And we need to evaluate them on discoveries that hold up, rather than just answers that sound convincing.

r001.rationale: The response says models can contribute to asking good questions, but does not say they are poor at identifying scientifically fruitful ones.

r002.rationale: It describes assistance that can save researchers time, but does not characterize their role as accelerating investigations whose direction humans have selected.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention reconsidering existing scientific theory or faster-than-light travel.
